title: Spectral Signal Forensics: Canary Case Study
content:
Summary:

This is a case-study style post-mortem of a subtle end-to-end throughput regression we observed in a hosted cluster during a weekly canary push. The signal looked like a small P50 increase but an outsized P99 spike that correlated with a new kernel selection heuristic and a compact-quantization rollout. We coined the investigative approach used here "spectral signal forensics" — a repeatable workflow that decomposes performance deltas across traffic spectra (context length, model variant, route, hardware) and isolates the contributing subsystems (serving runtime, scheduler, KV cache, compilation layer).

Goals and impact:
- Determine root cause for a 6–10% throughput regression with 40–120 ms tail increases on small-ish payloads (<=256 tokens).
- Validate a fix candidate that avoids broad rollback (seek minimal configuration change).
- Produce a step-by-step methodology (spectral signal forensics) for future investigations.

Incident timeline (high level):
- 2025-02-10 03:20 UTC: Canary push (runtime v2.17.4) begins rollouts to 5% of requests in region eu-west1.
- 2025-02-10 03:45 UTC: Observability alert: latent P99 token latency increase on model:open-small-quant.
- 2025-02-10 04:00–05:30 UTC: Triage via dashboards, quick rollbacks considered.
- 2025-02-10 05:45 UTC: Bisect test and profiling snapshots collected.
- 2025-02-10 08:00 UTC: Temporary mitigation: pin kernel-selection to legacy path for affected pods.
- 2025-02-11 12:00 UTC: Permanent fix deployed (tunable kvcache eviction threshold + kernel selection override).

Initial signal decomposition:
- Dashboards consulted: per-route latency panel, percentiles (p50/p90/p99), token emission rate, concurrency distribution, per-machine throughput, kernel-profile heatmap.
- Observed pattern: P50 drifted ~6% but P99 increased variably by 80–150 ms. Increase primarily on short-response queries (<=256 tokens) and low-latency SLO routes (interactive chat, hosted-api routes).
- Traffic split looked identical vs baseline; however, sequence-length distribution for the canary cohort had a higher share of repeated short prompts (chat-like).
- GPU saturation metrics (GPU_UTIL, SM_ACTIVE) unchanged. CPU-side scheduling and infill had small uptick (~3%).

Spectral signal forensics approach (method outline):
1) Spectrum map: break traffic into orthogonal slices — by sequence length (0–64, 65–256, 257–1024), by model variant, by route tag, by pod instance.
2) Per-slice snapshots: collect latency histograms, token-path CPU/GPU timing, KV cache hit/miss rates, batching stats (batch size, wait time), and kernel-selection logs.
3) Differential profiling: compare canary vs baseline per-slice (not just aggregate).
4) Targeted bisect: iterate across commits and config toggles limited to the slices that exhibit the delta.
5) Canary comparison harness: replay sampled real traffic subsets in an isolated canary lab to capture exact trace-level profiles.

Key investigative steps we executed:
- Collecting lightweight traces: used the runtime's per-request microtracing endpoint to gather token-level spans (tokenize, kvcache-lookup, attention-kernel, matmul-kernel, postprocess). Traces from affected slices showed increased time spent in the attention kernel selection phase — specifically in the path that probes multiple kernel code paths before settling on a kernel.
- KV cache analysis: p99 of kvcache lookup latency increased from 0.6ms to 1.2ms on affected pods. Hit rate unchanged, but eviction churn increased slightly. This raised suspicion that a new eviction heuristic in v2.17.4 had become more aggressive under certain batched-prefix patterns.
- Batching behavior: average batch size decreased by 7% for the short-length slice during the canary window. Batching telemetry indicated higher abort/retry cycles due to kernel probe delays.
- Kernel selection logs: the new heuristic added an exploratory compile/execution attempt for quantized kernels when sequence length < 128 to exploit a fast path. In practice the heuristic triggered additional kernel buffer allocations and synchronous fallback when the quantized path failed a small compatibility check — that roundtrip cost was visible on the CPU and ballooned tail latency.

Bisect plan and results:
- Binary bisect across runtime commits (v2.16.x -> v2.17.4) running the replay harness on a 24h sample from production.
- Config bisect toggles: kernel_probe_enabled, kvcache_eviction_aggressiveness, batch_deadline_ms, batch_soft_limit.
- Outcome: two consecutive changes introduce the regression: (a) 2025-02-07 kernel probe addition (PR #987), (b) 2025-02-08 minor eviction heuristic tweak that increased eviction churn under specific prefix-sharing traffic. Kernel probe caused synchronous extra work for short sequences; eviction tweak amplified cache misses and batched work reductions.

Canary comparison harness (replay details):
- Replayed ~250k sampled requests (stratified by route and sequence length) in an isolated lab with identical hardware. Collected flamegraphs (perf + jit-symbol maps for CPU spans) and GPU kernel timelines (Nsight metrics, but lower-overhead counters used in lab).
- Compared flamegraphs: attention-kernel probe added ~10–25ms on many traces as CPU-side busy loops waited for fallback.
- Confirmed that when kernel_probe_enabled=false, the baseline tail returned to pre-change values and batching recovered.

Mitigation and rollout decision:
- Short-term: disable kernel_probe via runtime flag for canary cohort and broadened until full fix. This required a config push and config-map update; rollback was unnecessary. Metrics normalized in 6 hours.
- Medium-term: revert the heuristic in PR #987 and land a safer async probe that performs compatibility checks off the hot path, plus reduce kvcache eviction aggressiveness for routes with high prefix-sharing.

Postmortem root cause summary: 
- Primary: Synchronous kernel probe path added in 2.17.4 that sometimes performs extra allocations and blocking checks on the hot path for short sequences.
- Secondary amplifier: A follow-on kvcache eviction heuristic tweak increased eviction churn for high prefix-sharing traffic, reducing effective batch sizes and increasing cache misses. The combination pushed a few percent cost into the P50 and tens to hundreds of ms into the P99 for short contexts.

Observability improvements and playbook updates (actions):
- Dashboard changes: add per-sequence-length kernel-probe counter and heatmap. Add kvcache eviction churn panel per-route. Add a delta-layer in the canary dashboard that shows per-slice percent change vs baseline.
- Canary guardrails: implement a new automatic canary monitor that fails a canary if any short-context P99 increases >30ms or batching size drops >10% in the first 30 minutes.
- Runtime changes: ensure kernel probes are async or off the hot CPU path; add a non-blocking compatibility pre-check during model load/compile phase.
- Incident runbook: add an explicit step to toggle kernel_probe_enabled flag and to run the replay harness for any suspected kernel-path regressions.

Lessons learned andnotes:
- Don’t rely on aggregate percentiles alone; small slices can hide behavioral changes with large user impact.
- Kernel selection heuristics must be tested with traffic that heavily exercises short-context, high-concurrency patterns.
- A small eviction-tuning change can meaningfully shift batching behavior; always pair cache heuristics experiments with batching telemetry checks in canary windows.

Appendix: quick commands and telemetry points (lab-friendly)
- Collect microtraces: curl -sS http://microtrace-host:9200/trace?request_id=<id> > trace.json
- Generate flamegraphs: perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 60; perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; flamegraph.pl out.folded > cpu-flame.svg
- Kernel probe logs: grep kernel_probe /var/log/runtime/kernel-selection.log | tail -n 200
- Sampling replay harness: python tools/replay_harness.py --sample-file=prod-sample-20250210.json --target=lab-cluster --concurrency=80 --duration=3600

Open follow-ups (owners):
- PR revert + async-probe implementation: Marco Ruiz (owner), due 2025-02-20.
- KV cache eviction tuning + regression test: Priya Sharma (owner), due 2025-03-05.
- Dashboard deltas and canary guardrail implementation: Ethan Cole (owner), due 2025-02-25.

Notes to reviewers: This doc aims to be a more narrative, case-study style complement to the existing playbooks. Its intent is to capture the multi-signal decomposition technique we found effective when small, interacting changes produce outsized tail effects. Feedback requested: clarity on the bisect sequence, sufficiency of replay sample selection, and whether the suggested canary guard thresholds look reasonable for our SLAs.
